function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** that you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository. I’ve written them with the assumption that the repo contains a very small Node.js app (e.g. `app.js`, `package.json`, maybe a `Dockerfile` that you want to replace). > **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to the repo from here, but the files below are ready for you to copy‑paste, commit, and push yourself. --- ## 1️⃣ Dockerfile Create or replace the existing `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following: ```dockerfile # Dockerfile # ------------------------------------ # Base image – lightweight Node runtime FROM node:18-alpine AS builder # Set working directory WORKDIR /usr/src/app # Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache COPY package*.json ./ # Install dependencies (including dev deps if you want tests) RUN npm ci # Copy the rest of the source code COPY . . # Build step (if you have a build script) # RUN npm run build # Production stage – keep the image small FROM node:18-alpine # Set working directory WORKDIR /usr/src/app # Copy only the production dependencies COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --only=production # Copy built files (or source if no build step) COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app . # Expose the port your app listens on EXPOSE 3000 # Default command CMD ["node", "app.js"] ``` > *Why this Dockerfile?* > * `node:18-alpine` is a small, production‑ready image. > * Multi‑stage build keeps the final image lean. > * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs. > * Exposes port **3000** – adjust if your app uses a different port. --- ## 2️⃣ Kubernetes YAML Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can keep it in a `k8s/` folder or at the repo root). Replace `` and `` with your actual registry and tag. ```yaml # k8s/deployment.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nodejs-welcome labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: nodejs-welcome template: metadata: labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: containers: - name: nodejs-welcome image: /nodejs-welcome: ports: - containerPort: 3000 env: - name: NODE_ENV value: production --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: nodejs-welcome spec: type: ClusterIP selector: app: nodejs-welcome ports: - protocol: TCP port: 80 targetPort: 3000 ``` > *What this does:* > * Deploys 2 replicas of your container. > * Exposes the app via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80 (internally forwards to 3000). > * You can change `replicas`, `service type`, or add more env vars as needed. --- ## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow Create a workflow file at `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`: ```yaml # .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml name: Build & Push Docker Image on: push: branches: - main jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: # Checkout the repo - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4 # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑arch support) - name: Set up Docker Buildx uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 # Log in to Docker Hub (or your registry) - name: Log in to Docker Hub uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }} # Build and push the image - name: Build and push Docker image uses: docker/build-push-action@v5 with: context: . push: true tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest # Optional: add a second tag with the commit SHA # tags: | # ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest # ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} # Optional: push a tag with the current date # - name: Tag image with date # run: | # DATE=$(date +%Y%m%d) # docker tag ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:$DATE # docker push ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:$DATE ``` ### What you need to do before the workflow runs | Item | How to set it up | |------|------------------| | `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` | Create a Docker Hub account (or use your registry). | | `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` | Generate a personal access token on Docker Hub with **write** permissions. | | Add both secrets to the repo:
`Settings → Secrets → Actions → New repository secret` | > *If you’re using GitHub Container Registry instead of Docker Hub, replace the login step with:* > ```yaml > - name: Log in to GHCR > uses: docker/login-action@v3 > with: > registry: ghcr.io > username: ${{ github.actor }} > password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} > ``` > And adjust the `tags:` line accordingly (`ghcr.io//nodejs-welcome:latest`). --- ## 4️⃣ Commit & Push Once you’ve added the three files above, run the following commands from the repo root: ```bash # Stage the new/updated files git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml # Commit with a descriptive message git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow" # Push to main git push origin main ``` > The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the push, build the image, and push it to your registry. --- ## 5️⃣ Quick Checklist - [ ] Dockerfile is in the repo root (or replace the existing one). - [ ] `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or wherever you prefer) contains the correct image name/tag. - [ ] `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml` has the right registry credentials set as secrets. - [ ] Commit and push the changes. Once pushed, you should see the workflow run in **Actions → All workflows → Build & Push Docker Image**. If it succeeds, your image will be available in the registry, and you can deploy it to any Kubernetes cluster using the manifest you just added. Happy coding! 🚀
